vignette: He sits on the edge of the examination chair, knees pressed together, eyes fixed on the scuffed floorboards. To anyone else, the room is quiet. To him, the air hums with potential threats. His hands, calloused from years of holding brushes and sanding poles, rest heavily in his lap. He is twenty-four, South Eastern Asian, with a quiet intensity that has hardened over the last eight months. He describes the night clearly, though his voice drops to a murmur. It is a Tuesday. The argument starts over something trivial—dishes left in the sink, a missed text—but the air in the apartment shifts, grows heavy and thin. He remembers turning to leave the kitchen, the floor tilting as a hand grabs his shoulder and yanks him back. Then the shove, the impact of his back against the doorframe, the sharp crack of his knuckles against the wall. He remembers the silence that follows, heavier than the shouting, the way his own breathing sounds too loud in his ears. He walks out into the rain, not knowing where to go, until his neighbor’s porch light finally becomes a destination. Since then, his world has narrowed. He works as a painter, a trade that once gave him rhythm and pride. Now, the smell of oil-based primer makes his throat close. He switches to watercolors and acrylics, keeping his workspace in the garage with the door cracked open. When he has to work on scaffolding or ladders, his hands shake slightly, and his mind races to the geometry of falls. He checks the structural integrity of every rung twice. At home, he sits with his back to the wall. Doors opening behind him make him startle, his spine going rigid before his brain catches up. He stops answering calls from people whose voices remind him of that night. He avoids certain neighborhoods, rerouting his commute three miles out of his way to pass the block where it happened. His current relationship endures, though the distance between them is measured in unspoken things. He watches his partner’s hands closely when they reach for objects on a high shelf, a flicker of panic crossing his face before he forces it down. He wakes at 3 a.m. most nights, heart hammering, convinced he hears footsteps in the hall. He tells himself it is just the house settling, but his jaw stays clenched until he makes tea. During work, when a client speaks sharply, his chest tightens and his brush slips, leaving a dark smear on freshly masked trim. He wipes it away quickly, pretending he did not notice. He tells himself he is just tired, that the weeks have been long. He sits now, breathing slowly, as he always does when the silence gets too loud. His therapist notes how he tracks the door, how his fingers trace the bristles of a sketching pencil he brought along to keep busy. The paint under his fingernails is half-moon crescents of titanium white and burnt umber. He speaks in careful paragraphs, measuring each word against the fear of being misunderstood. The room holds him, quiet and still, as he waits for the next question. He does not know yet how to name the weight he carries, but he continues to show up, brush in hand, one stroke at a time.
